abstract: Strada Institute's survey of 1,498 US executives and senior talent leaders, conducted March 3-22, 2026, provides employer-side evidence on how AI is affecting entry-level hiring. The findings challenge displacement narratives: 46% of employers that have at least explored AI report that it increased entry-level hiring in 2025, compared to only 13% reporting a decrease—a roughly 4-to-1 ratio favoring increased hiring. Looking ahead, employers are 2.7x more likely to expect AI will raise entry-level hiring in 2026 than cut it. Notably, 92% of surveyed employers are engaging with AI in some capacity. A perhaps counterintuitive finding is that AI literacy is ranked as the least important entry-level skill by employers, suggesting that organizations value domain expertise and foundational capabilities over AI-specific technical skills when hiring junior workers. The results indicate that, at least in the current phase, AI adoption is creating more entry-level positions than it eliminates, potentially by expanding what organizations can accomplish and lowering the cost of onboarding junior workers.
keyFindings: 46% of employers that have explored AI say it increased entry-level hiring in 2025, versus only 13% reporting a decrease—a 4-to-1 ratio favoring increased hiring.
Employers are 2.7x more likely to expect AI will raise entry-level hiring in 2026 than cut it, indicating continued optimism about AI-complementary job creation.
92% of surveyed employers are engaging with AI in some capacity, indicating near-universal organizational exploration of AI technologies.
AI literacy is ranked as the least important entry-level skill by employers, suggesting organizations prioritize domain expertise and foundational capabilities over AI-specific technical skills.
The survey captures employer intent and perception at a moment (March 2026) when AI adoption is widespread but labor market impacts are still emerging.
methodology: Survey of 1,498 US executives and senior talent leaders conducted March 3-22, 2026 by the Strada Institute. Survey captures self-reported impacts of AI on entry-level hiring levels (increased, decreased, no change), forward-looking hiring expectations, AI engagement status, and skill priority rankings for entry-level positions.
qualifiers: Self-reported employer perceptions may not align with actual hiring data—executives may overstate positive impacts or conflate correlation with causation. The 46% increase figure applies only to employers that have at least explored AI, excluding non-adopters who may have different employment patterns. Survey conducted during a period of relatively strong labor markets, which may inflate positive sentiment. Strada Institute focuses on workforce development, which may shape question framing. The survey does not distinguish between net new positions and redistributed entry-level roles. Forward-looking expectations (2.7x ratio) are intentions, not outcomes, and may not materialize if economic conditions change.
